Mr. Charles J. Oilebeke
Data Book of Total Energy Magazine lists 507 total energy systems currently in service, of which 428 include generation of electricity in all types of installations. The total installed generating capacity is over one million kilowatts. In Jamacia, New York, the Rochdale Village project has been in operation since Detember 1963. This installation which consists of two 6,000-kilowatt steam turbines, and two 3,000-kilowatt diesel engines serves apartments, shopping centers, and other service buildings. Under construction at the present time is Wingate Village in Indianapolis, Indiana, which when completed will consist of 1,250 apartments whose energy requirements will be provided by eight 500-kilowatt gas-engine generators. Enough design and practical operating experience have been accumulated to demonstrate the technical and economic criteria which must be satisfied before the full potential of the total energy concept can be realized.
To achieve its full economic potential, the heat requirements of the hot water and space heating and cooling components of a total energy system must balance to a substantial degree the heat in the exhaust gases or steam being rejected by the prime mover used in the generation of electricity. If the heat in the exhaust gases or steam is in excess of these requirements at any particular moment, some of the heat must be discarded or stored with a resultant drop in overall efficiency of the system. If the heat in the exhaust gases or steam in storage is not sufficient to match the heat demand for hot water or space heating and cooling or process steam, it is common practice to supply the deficiency from other sources.
It is often difficult to achieve a good balance between electrical and heat loads in a housing project because of the varying demand for electric service during the course of the day and night. Each total energy system is in fact a mini-electric utility system faced with the same problems of diversity of demand, reserve capacity, maintenance of equipment, and equipment breakdowns. But, whereas the central station can depend on the network for assistance in time of trouble, the total energy system usually must rely entirely on its own resources. On the other hand the reliability of a total energy system is not affected by external network disturbances against which electric network utility systems must protect themselves.
